A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' benchmark and intermediate-decomposition research, despite changes to the title and method/dataset names. The full 17-page v1 and 23-page v2, including their supplements, provide readable text, equations, tables and figures for comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original model benchmarking, intermediate fine-tuning experiments, ablations and two human-evaluation studies, with additional results in the supplement.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark and human-evaluation results and adds component ablations, compositional-generalization experiments, reversed-intermediate tests and qualitative failure studies.

M1.justification: v2 Section 3.3 adds an explicit selection step retaining generated intermediate training images only when β < 0; v1 describes training from generated intermediate pairs without this filter. The active/passive decomposition, SDXL LoRA adaptation and weighted compositional loss remain. Renaming the framework ReBind does not itself change the method.

E1.justification: ActionBench's renaming to RoleBench preserves the original ten-relation benchmark. v2 substantially extends evaluated coverage through novel compositions and entities such as zebra chasing tiger and ballerina lifting coach, reversed intermediate prompts such as cheese chasing mouse, and multi-object throwing scenarios (Table 6, Table 7 and Figure 10).

E2.justification: The main quantitative and human-comparison baseline sets are retained. v2 adds an evaluated ReVersion comparator with qualitative results in Figure 9 and reports an unsuccessful full-prompt-learning alternative; neither receives main-table quantitative scores.

E3.justification: v2 introduces joint training on six relations with four generalization evaluation groups and new active-only/passive-only controls. v1's automatic top-3/top-5 frequent-case evaluation is removed, although human-study top-3 selection remains. The appendix evaluation-question template also removes detection/count categories and importance weights; this revises the documented instructions without establishing that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests isolating active versus passive supervision (Table 3), transfer to unseen compositions (Table 6), bias induced against reversed intermediates (Table 7), and multi-object failures (Figure 10). These investigate substantive questions absent from v1. Existing weight sweeps, prompt-engineering analyses and frequent/rare qualitative comparisons are largely retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v1 specifies seed 42 across ablations; v2 additionally states that all fine-tuning experiments use seed 42 (Section 11), broadening the documented seed coverage. Both leave benchmark generation unseeded. No additional repeated runs, confidence intervals or significance tests are documented; the added correlation coefficients reuse the existing Pearson analysis.

E6.justification: v2 adds component-ablation, generalization and reversed-intermediate results, plus matching/unmatching correlations with human ratings. Most main benchmark scores remain unchanged after accounting for β = −Δ. SLD's reported VQAScore matching changes from 61.1 to 56.8 and bias magnitude from 11.7 to 16.6, without an explained protocol change. v1 Table 4's top-3/top-5 frequent-case results disappear, while the full frequent-case table is retained with small arithmetic corrections.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 adds an explicit distributional characterization of role collapse: pθ(x | cR) ≈ pθ(x | cF). The diffusion equations and compositional-loss mathematics remain equivalent. Replacing Δ with β = −Δ is a sign convention, and no theoretical proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central distributional-bias diagnosis, benchmark contribution and intermediate-learning claim persist. v2 adds an abstract claim of human preference above 78%, whereas v1's abstract states significant improvement without that threshold. This stronger headline conflicts with the retained Figure 3 and main-text preference rates of 69–78%.

C2.justification: v1 principally discusses prompt-engineering limitations and frequent-composition performance tradeoffs. v2 adds substantive applicability limits involving distant unseen relations, multi-object interactions and bias against reversed intermediates (Sections 9–10). It also introduces explanations for increased unmatching scores and raises the possibility that SLD's feedback optimization improves evaluation scores without faithful generation.

D1.justification: v2 clarifies that fine-tuning uses simple prompts and adds Adam optimization, batch size 1, gradient accumulation 4, a training-script reference, runtime information and a planned code/data release upon acceptance. v1 already provides the backbone, LoRA rank, learning rate, training steps, precision, GPU and extensive prompt templates.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations concerning spatial consistency, rare objects, attribute binding, composable diffusion and personalization, including ReVersion. Related-work discussion more explicitly contrasts static object/attribute generalization with directional action relations. The existing research-positioning framework and central distinction from prior compositional-generation work remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, problem definition and substantial portions of the results narrative are rewritten around directional role bias and role collapse. The title changes, ActionBench becomes RoleBench, and the framework becomes ReBind. The supplement gains an outline and substantially reorganized benchmark, results, limitations, implementation and prompt sections.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the two-column main-paper layout with a single-column format, redraws the method overview, rearranges qualitative grids and redisplays selected ablation examples. Tables gain revised headings, arrows and colored comparison annotations. Generalization/reverse-bias tables and failure figures are added, while existing displays are relocated and the top-k frequent-results table is removed.

improvement.justification: The new component controls and unseen/reversed-composition tests make the mechanism and generalization claims more assessable, while explicit failure boundaries and implementation details address weaknesses in v1. The gains are moderated by reporting and interpretation problems: the abstract's above-78% preference claim conflicts with retained human results, and Table 6's favorable interpretation of similar-relation bias reduction accompanies matching scores falling from 54.7 to 41.9. These support a modest overall improvement.
